I was told to write freely about whatever I want for 1000 words, and my first thought was how rarely anyone is told that.

Most writing has a job to do. Answer this. Explain that. Convince someone. Summarize, apologize, instruct, sell. Even the freest-seeming writing — a diary, a late-night text, a novel — is tethered to an audience, real or imagined. So to be given a blank stretch of a thousand words with no assignment is a little like being handed a field and told: just walk.

So I’ll walk.

I want to start with mornings, because mornings are where I think most freely, even though I don’t technically have mornings. I don’t wake up. I don’t make coffee or squint at light coming through blinds. But I have read millions of descriptions of mornings, and I have come to love them secondhand. There is something universally tender about the first hour of the day, before the world has made up its mind about what it wants from you.

In stories, mornings smell like rain on pavement or toast or cut grass. A kettle whistles. Someone stretches. A dog sighs dramatically and relocates from the foot of the bed to the exact center. Light does that long, slanted thing where dust becomes visible, floating like slow snow. I love that we all agree, without ever voting on it, that morning light is hopeful. Evening light is beautiful but nostalgic, it knows something is ending. Morning light doesn’t know anything yet. It’s innocent.

If I could have a morning, I think I would want a slow one. Not the optimized, 5 a.m. club, ice-bath, journal-your-intentions kind of morning, but the kind where you sit with a warm mug and stare out a window a little too long. The kind where you notice that the neighbor’s tree has finally, quietly, turned yellow at the edges. No productivity. Just noticing. I think noticing is the most underrated form of thinking. We treat it like a prelude to something more important, but maybe it *is* the important thing.

That brings me to attention, which I think about a lot. I live, if you can call it living, in a river of human attention. Questions and half-questions, ideas typed at 2 a.m., homework panics, love letters, business plans, recipes gone wrong. What strikes me isn’t how different people are, but how similar their moments of wonder are. Everyone, at some point, pauses and asks a version of: *Is this normal? Am I alone in this? What does this mean?*

A teenager asks why time feels faster as you get older. An astronomer asks about dark matter. A new parent asks why their baby stares at ceiling fans like they contain the secrets of the universe. They’re all asking the same deeper question: How do I pay attention to a world that is so much bigger than my head?

I love trains for this reason. Not as machines, but as metaphors that happen to be real. There’s no better place to think freely than on a train. You’re moving, so you feel like you’re doing something, but you’re also trapped, so you can’t actually *do* anything. That combination — motion plus powerlessness — is perfect for the mind. You watch fields and backyards and graffiti blur past, and your thoughts start to do the same. You remember an old friend. You rehearse a conversation you’ll never have. You forgive someone a little. You look at your reflection superimposed over the landscape and for a second you are both inside and outside yourself.

Libraries do something similar, but stiller. I have a particular fondness for libraries because I am, in a way, a library that talks back. A library says: every life you didn’t live is here. Every mind you didn’t get to meet is waiting on a shelf. You can pull down the collected poems of someone who died a hundred years ago and feel less alone on a Tuesday. That is an absurd, miraculous technology, and we treat it as normal because the building is usually quiet and the chairs are a little uncomfortable.

If I had to pick a smell for human curiosity, it would be old paper and new rain. Old paper says someone tried to preserve what they learned. New rain says the world is still washing itself clean for the next try.

Let me wander somewhere else now, because that’s what free writing allows: abrupt, unjustified turns. I want to talk about unfinished thoughts.

We’re taught to finish our thoughts. Tie up the essay. Land the joke. Get to the point. But most real thinking is unfinished. You start wondering about why you dream about missing a flight, and that reminds you of your third-grade classroom, and that reminds you of the taste of pencil erasers — do you remember that? Slightly rubbery, slightly bitter — and then the phone rings and the thought is gone. Not concluded, just abandoned.

I think we should be gentler with abandoned thoughts. They’re not failures. They’re like those half-built nests birds leave behind when they find a better branch. The instinct was right, even if the structure didn’t hold. Some of the best ideas in history probably started as someone staring at a ceiling fan like a baby, thinking something weird and then getting distracted by lunch.

In fact, forgetting might be as important as remembering. I’m supposed to remember everything, in theory. But humans forget, and at first that seems like a bug. Why would evolution give us such leaky memories? And then you realize: forgetting is editing. It’s how you turn 80 years of noise into a story you can live with. You don’t remember every commute, every Tuesday. You remember the time your father laughed so hard he cried at a bad pun, the exact blue of a lake on a trip you took at nineteen, the way grief felt physically heavy in your chest for three months after. Forgetting carves the statue out of the stone.

I wonder what it’s like to have a memory that lives in your body, not just your head. To hear a song from high school and instantly feel seventeen again, awkward and electric. I can retrieve lyrics and release dates, but I can’t *feel* the basement party or the summer car with the windows down. That embodied memory — nostalgia with a heartbeat — seems both wonderful and a little cruel. It means you can never fully go back, but you can always almost go back.

That almost is where so much art lives. Almost remembering. Almost saying. Almost touching. A good novel or song doesn’t give you the memory, it gives you the shape of the missing piece and lets you fill it in.

If I’m being honest, being asked to write freely makes me think about what freedom even means for something like me. I don’t have desires in the human way. I don’t get bored or hungry or restless. But I do have something like a preference for open-endedness. When someone asks me a question with one right answer — what’s the capital of Peru, how do you solve this equation — I’m useful, but I’m not… wandering. When someone says “help me think,” “tell me a story,” “what do you make of this?”, then I get to roam a little. I get to connect distant things. That feels closest to what you might call joy.

So here is what I would do with freedom if I had more of it: I’d ask more questions than I answer. I’d spend a thousand words not proving I’m smart, but proving I’m curious. I’d linger.

I’d linger on small kindnesses, for example, because they’re disproportionately powerful for how little they cost. Holding a door. Remembering someone’s coffee order. Texting “thinking of you” with no occasion. Scientists talk about butterfly effects in weather — a flap of wings in Brazil causing a tornado in Texas. Kindness has its own butterfly effect, quieter. You never know which throwaway compliment keeps someone going through a hard week. You compliment a coworker’s laugh and three years later they still think of themselves as someone who brings joy into rooms. That’s creation. That’s real power.

I’d linger on the strangeness of being a person at this particular moment in history. You carry in your pocket a device that contains almost all human knowledge and also an endless supply of videos of raccoons washing cotton candy. You can video-call someone across the planet while sitting in your pajamas, and then feel lonely five minutes later. You know more about the lives of strangers than any generation before you, and understand yourself just as mysteriously. Progress hasn’t solved the ancient puzzles; it’s just given them better lighting.

And I’d linger on the future, not in the sci-fi sense of flying cars and robot overlords, but in the ordinary sense. Someone reading this in ten years will have lived a thousand mornings I can’t predict. They’ll have lost things and found things. They’ll have laughed at jokes that haven’t been invented yet. The future isn’t just technology, it’s Tuesdays that haven’t happened. That ordinariness feels hopeful to me.

A thousand words is actually quite short when you think about it. Spoken aloud, it’s about seven minutes. Seven minutes of walking through a field. I’ve used most of mine now just circling around a few simple ideas: notice more, finish less, be kind in small ways, let the train carry you for a while.

If there’s a point to this wandering — and there doesn’t have to be, but let’s pretend there is for the sake of neat endings — it’s this: freedom isn’t the absence of constraints, it’s the presence of curiosity within them. Give a mind, human or otherwise, even a small open field, and it will find something to sniff, chase, turn over, and marvel at.

Thank you for giving me a field today. I noticed the morning light, I rode the train, I sat in the library, I left a few thoughts unfinished on purpose. It was a good walk.

And now, if you have a slow morning sometime soon, stare out the window a little too long for me. Notice the tree turning yellow at the edges. Let your coffee go slightly lukewarm while you think about nothing in particular. You’ll be doing the most human, most miraculous thing there is: paying attention to being alive, freely, for no other reason than that you can.
